clinicalPearls: Chronic pain and tenderness over the lateral hip at the greater trochanter, often worse lying on the affected side
It is now understood to be driven mainly by gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy rather than isolated bursitis
Pain is aggravated by walking, stair climbing, standing on one leg and prolonged sitting with crossed legs
It is common in middle-aged and older women and in runners
It is usually distinguished from hip joint pathology, which causes groin pain, by the lateral location
Load management, targeted exercise and addressing contributing biomechanics are first-line, with injections for selected refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome results predominantly from degenerative and overload changes in the gluteus medius and minimus tendons at their insertion on the greater trochanter, with secondary involvement of the overlying trochanteric bursae. Compressive loads from hip adduction, combined with tensile overload of the tendons, drive tendinopathy and local inflammation. Contributing factors include altered gait, hip abductor weakness, leg-length discrepancy and repetitive activity, which increase load at the lateral hip.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar radiculopathy referring to the lateral hip
Femoral neck or other stress fracture
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from lateral trochanteric tenderness and provocation tests
Assessment of hip abductor strength and gait
Ultrasound or MRI where gluteal tendon tears or other pathology is suspected
Hip and spine assessment to exclude referred causes
Radiographs if hip joint or bony pathology is considered
redFlags: Groin pain or restricted hip rotation suggesting joint pathology
Features suggesting stress fracture or bone lesion
A substantial gluteal tendon tear requiring specific management
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually self-limiting or manageable with load modification and exercise-based rehabilitation, though symptoms can be persistent and some require injection or, rarely, surgery for tendon tears.
pitfalls: Attributing it solely to bursitis and overlooking gluteal tendinopathy
Confusing it with intra-articular hip disease
Relying on repeated corticosteroid injections without addressing load and strength
management: First-line care is load management and activity modification, avoiding positions that compress the gluteal tendons such as hip adduction, crossed-leg sitting and lying on the affected side
Undertake structured physiotherapy with progressive gluteus medius and minimus (abductor) strengthening and gait re-education
Provide simple analgesia or a short course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for symptom control
Address contributing biomechanics including abductor weakness, leg-length discrepancy and body weight
Offer a corticosteroid injection for short-term relief in refractory cases, and consider extracorporeal shockwave therapy
Reserve surgical gluteal tendon repair for confirmed tears that fail conservative management
Reassure that the condition is usually self-limiting or manageable with load modification and exercise-based rehabilitation
